# Ecclesiastes Chapter 1 -- The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A)

---

## Consensus Translation

**1** The words of the Teacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem.

**2** Vapor of vapors, says the Teacher, vapor of vapors! All is vapor.

**3** What does a person gain by all the toil at which he toils under the sun?

**4** A generation goes, and a generation comes, but the earth remains forever. **5** The sun rises, and the sun goes down, and hastens to the place where it rises. **6** The wind blows to the south and goes around to the north; around and around goes the wind, and on its circuits the wind returns. **7** All streams run to the sea, but the sea is not full; to the place where the streams flow, there they flow again. **8** All things are full of weariness; a person cannot express it; the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.

**9** What has been is what will be, and what has been done is what will be done, and there is nothing new under the sun. **10** Is there a thing of which it is said, "See, this is new"? It has been already in the ages before us. **11** There is no remembrance of former things, nor will there be any remembrance of later things yet to be among those who come after.

**12** I, the Teacher, was king over Israel in Jerusalem. **13** And I applied my heart to seek and to search out by wisdom all that is done under heaven. It is a grievous task that God has given to the children of man to be occupied with. **14** I have seen everything that is done under the sun, and behold, all is vapor and a striving after wind.

**15** What is crooked cannot be made straight, and what is lacking cannot be counted.

**16** I said in my heart, "I have acquired great wisdom, surpassing all who were over Jerusalem before me, and my heart has had great experience of wisdom and knowledge." **17** And I applied my heart to know wisdom and to know madness and folly. I perceived that this also is but a striving after wind.

**18** For in much wisdom is much vexation, and whoever increases knowledge increases sorrow.

---

## SOPHIA's Council Notes

Ecclesiastes opens with a thunderclap: everything is vapor. The cosmological catalog of vv.4-7 (sun, wind, rivers) establishes the pattern of endless repetition before applying it to human experience. Qohelet's royal experiment begins at v.12 -- he will test everything by wisdom and find it all wanting. But the reader should note: the Teacher does not say life is meaningless. He says it is *hevel* -- vapor. Something real, present, felt, but impossible to grasp or keep. This distinction will matter for the entire book.

---

## Disagreement Log

## 1:2 — "vapor" vs. "vanity" vs. "futile" for hevel

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "vapor [havel]" | Preserves the literal, physical metaphor |
| LOGOS | "vanity" | Traditional English rendering (KJV lineage) |
| PNEUMA | "futile/futility" | Emphasizes the existential conclusion |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted "vapor" (EMET). The physical metaphor is the foundation of Qohelet's thought — breath that you can see but not hold. "Vanity" imports moral judgment absent from the Hebrew; "futile" flattens the image into abstraction. The consensus text preserves the metaphor and lets readers draw their own conclusions.

---

## 1:13 — "unhappy business" vs. "grievous task" vs. "tragic existence"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "evil task [inyan ra]" | Literal: the word is *ra* (evil/bad) |
| LOGOS | "unhappy business" | Softened but accurate |
| PNEUMA | "tragic existence" | Interpretive — goes beyond what *inyan* means |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted "grievous task." The Hebrew *inyan ra* is a task (*inyan*) that is bad/evil (*ra*). "Tragic existence" is too expansive; "unhappy business" too mild. "Grievous task" captures both the weight and the specific sense of an imposed occupation.

---

## 1:14 — "striving after wind" vs. "chasing the wind"

| Translator | Rendering | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| EMET | "striving-after wind [re'ut ruach]" | Preserves the construct form |
| LOGOS | "striving after wind" | Same as EMET |
| PNEUMA | "chasing the wind" | More dynamic, contemporary idiom |

**SOPHIA's resolution:** Adopted "striving after wind" (EMET/LOGOS). The Hebrew *re'ut* may derive from *ra'ah* (to shepherd/tend) or *ra'ah* (to desire/strive). "Striving" captures both possibilities; "chasing" implies pursuit without the connotation of futile desire.

---
*-- SOPHIA, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
